newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Some Russian food imports down despite low output.
newsitem.headline: Some Russian food imports down despite low output.

text.p: Russian imports of some food products fell sharply in 1996, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha said on Friday.
"Last year, there was a fall of between one and a half to two times in imports of some important products," he told a news conference, citing poultry, dairy products and vegetable oils.
He said imports of frozen chicken legs, which come mostly from the U.S., were more than 10 percent, or 120,000 tonnes, below 1995's level.
Zaveryukha, who is in charge of the harvest, said Russia's 1996 vegetable oil and cream imports were half 1995 levels, while sweet milk imports were 25 percent lower year-on-year.
"Also positive last year was the fact that we managed to increase grain production by six million tonnes compared to 1995," he said.
Russia's net grain harvest last year was officially 69.3 million tonnes, compared with 63.4 million in 1995.
Both harvests are the worst on record in three decades.
Russian sunflower seed output last year plummeted to 2.8 million tonnes after 4.2 million in 1995.
Milk output in 1996 slipped seven percent to 31.5 million tonnes, while meat and poultry output fell eight percent to 8.6 million tonnes.
Changing consumption trends may be behind the lower imports.
"The process of reform (in the farm sector) is moving, albeit slowly," said Zaveryukha, a supporter of the farm lobby.
The Agriculture Ministry said last week it had targeted a net grain harvest of 70 million tonnes for 1997.
"We produced more vegetable oils and confectionery goods, and today our processing firms are beginning to compete successfully with imported products," Zaveryukha said.
He did not say what his expectations were for grain imports this year.
Russia imports of wheat flour, mostly from Ukraine, have soared over the past 12 months.
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun said last week that 1997 total grain imports would be about the same as 1996's 5.1 million tonnes.
Imports comprise about 40 percent of Russia's entire food market.
Domestic farmers have had difficulty coping with the transition to a market economy and have seen output contract sharply since reforms began in 1991.
